A clock that keeps every minute has to g: A clock that keeps every minute has to get them from somewhere. Each swing of the pendulum takes one from someone in the house. That is why candles here burn so fast. It is why we all grew old so quickly.

Every chore in this house is written in: Every chore in this house is written in the Book of Rounds: wind the clock at twelve, bank the furnace, lock the crypt, ring the bell at one. The first line is in the clockmaker's own hand, and the ink is three hundred years old.

Every night at twelve I light Tallow, sa: Every night at twelve I light Tallow, say good evening and blow him out again. A year of that and he will light himself, like everything else here. I have chalked the cellar floor for him and hidden what I can in the walls, sealed with wax so he knows where to knock.

I took the wax from the cellar while Mot: I took the wax from the cellar while Mother slept, only the clean top, and an old wick from the chapel. He came out stubby and lopsided, and cried wax when I struck the match. I have named him Tallow. Mother will want him back. She can't have him.
In this house, anything done every night: In this house, anything done every night for long enough starts to do itself. The organ plays itself. The pot stirs itself. Mind your habits here. They will outlive you.

Martha Fenn, aged fourteen: one good dre: Martha Fenn, aged fourteen: one good dress and a cold. That was me, my first night in this house. At twelve the clock struck and the whole house got up. Cook said staring was rude and handed me a broom.

Something lives in the gaps between the: Something lives in the gaps between the ticks. Cook called it the Hour Fiend. It eats the minutes you waste, and it wants the clock to strike two. At two the rounds end, and anything still burning goes out.

Tallow, my knees won't do the stairs any: Tallow, my knees won't do the stairs any more, so the climb is yours. Go up past the bells and tell them all they can stop. Don't cry, you'll only drip. You are the bravest thing in this house. Love, Martha.
The Gaoler locks the crypt every night,: The Gaoler locks the crypt every night, though nobody living goes in. The Sexton measures everyone who comes to dinner, just in case. When the crypt ran out of room, the old bones were stacked in a corner. The stack has opinions now.
The Head Librarian has shushed this hous: The Head Librarian has shushed this house for two hundred years. Nobody saw her come in, and nobody dares ask her to leave. She once shushed Cook for laughing in the kitchen, two floors down. Cook did her laughing in the garden after that.
The Keeper of Hours keeps it.
The Kitchen, the Library, the Attic: lit: The Kitchen, the Library, the Attic: lit again after all these years.
The clockmaker let the room under the ce: The clockmaker let the room under the cellar stairs to pay for his clock. The lodger never left, and never paid. Every candle end this house ever burnt has run down there into one warm pink pool. We call her Mother. She counts every drip.
The family went to the seaside in my thi: The family went to the seaside in my third summer and never came back. They sent letters, then money, then nothing. We kept the house for them anyway. That is what keeping a house means, I suppose.
The kitchen light is on. Somebody is exp: The kitchen light is on. Somebody is expected.
The kitchen light is on. You can finally: The kitchen light is on. You can finally rest.
The last candle in the cellar.
The maids held a seance in the back parl: The maids held a seance in the back parlour to ask the house what it wanted. Every lodger in the house answered at once. It took a week to get the soot out of the curtains. We did not ask again.
The man who built this house made clocks: The man who built this house made clocks, and he was afraid of one thing: a wasted minute. So he built a clock to keep every minute in the house, and a brass keeper to wind it. He never told it when to stop.
The pot cools. The organ breathes out. T: The pot cools. The organ breathes out. The Gaoler hangs up its keys.

We buried Mr. Pennock, the organist, on: We buried Mr. Pennock, the organist, on a Tuesday. That night the organ played the whole service by itself and got the hymn numbers wrong, just like he did. It has not missed a service since. The choir sing along. Their faces have run a bit.
When I came there were nine of us below: When I came there were nine of us below stairs. One by one they married, or left, or were buried, the way people do. The house never noticed. It just went on doing their chores without them.

Wilf, the boot boy, slept in the coal bi: Wilf, the boot boy, slept in the coal bin because it was the warmest bed in the house. He slept there so long the house forgot he was a boy. Snuffing a lodger only puts it to bed until twelve. Be gentle with Wilf anyway. He hated the dark.
